posts.author: ron olson
posts.content_md: There’s something curious about the jpeg/holography contest that I hope hasn’t escaped everyone’s attention. While the theme is “dogs” there isn’t a single holographic image of a dog in the competition. A note of explanation: my own jpeg entry was submitted two days late and therefore (my heart obviously wasn’t really in it anyway) rejected. All the images are of dog depictions (some very well done indeed) but it got me to wondering if there was a photographic competition with “dogs” as the theme, what would be the odds of not having a single real dog entry? Pretty slim. For this forum, wouldn’t a better (more appropriate) classification be “still-lifes” and if next year the theme is “dragons” will it really make all that much difference as to the way the project is approached?

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Ron, first of all I have to say your work is fantastic!!! 

But if we narrowed down the contest rules to not include depictions of dogs there would only be a hologram or two entered (I assume you mean real dogs as in pulsed or stereograms).

Consider how many entries made it and how many members are on this forum. It surely was not because of a lack of prizes. I believe keeping the contest as open as possible and just having some simple theme does allow the largest group the possibility to enter.

posts.author: ron olson
posts.content_md:
John thank you for the favorable comment - I agree with your observation regarding the contest. My point was to be realistic in targeting the competition to the predominant hardware in use. For me, imaging dogs brings up a completely different set of problems than imaging (for example) tanks of fish or a snow covered tree-top. If you're imaging a ceramic dog or a ceramic whale, it's pretty much the same thing except you go to a different garage sale, art gallery or model maker as a necessary first step. Still lifes are obviously an extremely vital component within art and can be every bit as dramatic as images of living subjects. My own piece "Buddha" is one of my most popular and "Protea with Anthuriums" is one of my personal favorites. I feel that the broader category allows more latitude for creativity without the somewhat dubious sub-category "dogs". I believe Michael's intention is to urge the creation of new works and opening the category to the broader definition could invite recycled pieces (like my own "Rosie" imaged almost 10 years ago). "New Still-Lifes" would seem to better address the goals of the contest and the strengths of the technique as practiced by the vast majority of forum contributors. 

I would add that my only regret in not being allowed into the competition is that I don't have a chance to finish third and win Frank DeFreitas' CD.

posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md: Hey Ron, its always intriguing to read your posts. If you made an entry for the contest(and would be most likely to win) ,wouldn’t you feel a little like the 5 year old playing on the four old soccer team???

posts.author: ron olson
posts.content_md:
Dave,

Maybe a little but I would use the analogy of the guy who's got a camera with lots of lenses and accessories competing against guys using a fixed lens and fewer accessories. There's no guarantees that the former will beat the latter - it's just that because of his hardware, he's probably got more artistic freedom regarding what he shoots. On the rare occasion when I'm asked, I point out that holography is akin to car racing: if you're really serious, you'll eventually have to bite the bullet and get a fast machine. It was, none the less, a good observation on your part that I'm at least 20% older than I should be.
